a: long untroubled peace and freedom from the hardships of war
t: A word marked as corrupt: what did the Latin say?
p: Fisher marks 'labor' as corrupt; the older English reads it as 'hardships of war'.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus), with the obelus (†) before the word
readings.en: undisturbed rest and the †labor† of men inexperienced in war
readings.plain: long untroubled peace and freedom from the hardships of war

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: the exemption from the hardships of war
readings.plain: long untroubled peace and freedom from the hardships of war

why: The dagger before labor is the editor's sign that the word is probably corrupt, so no reading of it is certain. The Conversational English Translation follows Church and Brodribb's sense, which fits the sentence: rested troops set against Vespasian's tested ones. If labor is wrong, the translation would still say that Mucianus's men had not met war, and only the word 'hardships' would change.

a: the soldiers' indiscipline, laziness and luxury
p: The Latin names the soldiers' vices; the older English says 'these men.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.plain: the soldiers' indiscipline, laziness and luxury

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: these men are quarrelsome, indolent and profligate
readings.plain: the quarrelsome, lazy and wasteful habits of these men

why: The Latin has three nouns in a row that go with the soldiers (militis), so the vices belong to the armies, not to the two emperors.

a: pointed to her womb
p: The Latin has the woman point to her womb; the older English softens it to 'bosom.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: The Latin word uterum means womb and gives the sense of her answer: he is hidden where he was born.

a: a thousand men from the detachments
p: The Latin has 'a thousand men of the detachments (vexillarii)'; the older English has 'veterans.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.en: a thousand men of the detachments
readings.plain: a thousand men from the detachments

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: Vexillarii can mean men of a detachment, or re-enlisted veterans serving under their own standard (Wikipedia, "Vexillarius"). The Conversational English Translation takes 'detachment'; Church and Brodribb took 'veterans'. The Latin word allows both.

a: detachment of the 13th legion
p: The Latin has 'a detachment (vexillum) of the 13th legion'; the older English has 'the veterans.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: Vexillum names the detachment's flag and so the detachment. Men under a vexillum could be a detachment or re-enlisted veterans under their own standard (Wikipedia, "Vexillarius"), so Church and Brodribb's 'veterans' is a possible sense. The Conversational English Translation takes 'detachment'.

a: the Padus and the Arda meet
p: Fisher's Latin names the river Arda; the older English has the Addua.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.en: of the Padus and the Arda
readings.plain: the Padus and the Arda meet

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: the confluence of the Padus and Addua
readings.plain: the Padus and the Addua meet

why: The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin as printed in Fisher's text, which names the Arda. The older English reads Addua, a different river name.

a: the 37th year of his age
p: Tacitus says the 37th year; Plutarch says 37 and Suetonius 38.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus); these words close Latin 2:49, and the site follows the English verse division
readings.en: in the thirty-seventh year of his age

readings.w: Suetonius, Otho 11 (English text at LacusCurtius)

why: The Latin of Tacitus reads 'the thirty-seventh year.' Plutarch (Otho 18.2) also says 37. Suetonius's different count is a different ancient account, not a manuscript reading.

a: Ferentium
p: The Latin has Ferentio (Ferentium); the older English has Ferentinum.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: The Latin ablative Ferentio gives the nominative Ferentium. Suetonius also places Otho's ancestors at Ferentium (Otho 1).

a: 8,000 men picked from the army of Britain
p: The Latin says 8,000 men picked from the army of Britain; the older English says a 'British conscription.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.orig: e Britannico exercitu delecta octo milia
readings.en: eight thousand chosen from the army of Britain
readings.plain: 8,000 men picked from the army of Britain

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: Delecta means chosen, and exercitu means army. The men were picked from the soldiers already in Britain.

a: gladiator schools and the arena
p: The Latin names the gladiator school and the arena; the older English has 'public entertainments.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: appearing in public entertainments, or in the arena

why: Ludus means a gladiators' school here. The older English widens it to all public shows.

a: in the manner of a king
t: Greeting a king, or a 'barbarous despot'?
p: The Latin has them sacrifice in the manner of a king; the older English adds 'barbarous despot.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.plain: in the manner of a king

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: as if to greet some barbarous despot
readings.plain: as if to greet some barbarous despot

why: The Latin has no word for barbarous or despot. It says only that they acted as people do for a king.

a: Valerius Marinus
p: The Latin names Valerius Marinus, whom Galba had named consul; the older English has Valerius Maximus.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: The Latin text has Marinum. The Conversational English Translation uses one name for this man across the Histories.

a: Galba's family portraits
p: The Latin says Vespasian yielded to Galba's ancestral images; the older English says 'the prestige of Galba's family.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.en: you even gave way to Galba's images

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: You have already yielded to the prestige even of Galba's family

why: Imagines were the wax masks and portraits of a noble family's ancestors, the sign of its rank. The older English gives the sense, not the word.

a: July 3rd
p: Tacitus has the army of Judea swear on 3 July; the editor of Suetonius reads Suetonius's date as 11 July.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.en: the fifth day before the Nones of July

readings.w: Suetonius, Vespasian 6.3 (text 'fifth day before the Ides of July'; the date 11 July is the editor's reading, note 16 at LacusCurtius)

why: Tacitus (2:79) names the fifth day before the Nones, 3 July. Suetonius (Vespasian 6.3) names the fifth day before the Ides, which his editor reads as 11 July. The two writers give different dates, eight days apart. No source cited for this page explains the difference.

a: 13,000 men from the detachments
p: The Latin has 13,000 men of the detachments; the older English has 'veterans.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: As at 2:18. Vexillarii can mean men of a detachment, or re-enlisted veterans serving under their own standard (Wikipedia, "Vexillarius"). The Conversational English Translation takes 'detachment'; Church and Brodribb took 'veterans'. The Latin word allows both.

a: Tampius Flavianus held Pannonia and Pompeius Silvanus Dalmatia
p: The Latin names Tampius Flavianus and Pompeius Silvanus; the older English has Titus Ampius Flavianus and Poppaeus Silvanus.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.plain: Tampius Flavianus held Pannonia and Pompeius Silvanus Dalmatia

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.plain: Titus Ampius Flavianus held Pannonia and Poppaeus Silvanus Dalmatia

why: The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin form and uses it in every book where the names appear (Books 2 to 4).

a: So he went up to the Capitol
p: The Latin says he went up to the Capitol; the older English says he 'entered the capital.'

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.plain: So he went up to the Capitol

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: The Latin word is Capitolium, the hill and temple of Jupiter.

a: Publilius Sabinus
p: The Latin has Publilium Sabinum; the older English has Publius Sabinus.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)

why: The Latin form is used for this man in all five books.

a: Asiaticus, Flavus and Rufinus, leaders of the Gauls
t: Is Asiaticus one of the Gallic leaders?
p: In the Latin, Asiaticus is listed with Flavus and Rufinus as leaders of the Gauls; the older English splits him off.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.orig: Asiaticus et Flavus et Rufinus duces Galliarum
readings.en: Asiaticus and Flavus and Rufinus, leaders of the Gauls
readings.plain: Asiaticus, Flavus and Rufinus, leaders of the Gauls

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: Asiaticus, and Flavius and Rufinus, the Gallic chieftains
readings.plain: Asiaticus, and Flavius and Rufinus, the Gallic chieftains

why: The Latin has one list of three names. The verse does not say whether this Asiaticus is Vitellius's freedman of 2:57 and 2:95.

a: the detachments of the 1st, 4th, 15th and 16th legions
p: The Latin lists detachments of the 1st, 4th, 15th and 16th; the older English lists veterans of the 4th, 10th and 16th.

readings.w: Fisher's Latin text (Oxford Classical Text, 1911, Perseus)
readings.orig: vexilla primae, quartae, quintaedecimae, sextaedecimae legionum
readings.en: detachments of the first, fourth, fifteenth, sixteenth legions
readings.plain: the detachments of the 1st, 4th, 15th and 16th legions

readings.w: Church and Brodribb's English (1864, Perseus)
readings.en: the veteran troops of the 4th, 10th, and 16th legions
readings.plain: the veteran troops of the 4th, 10th and 16th legions

why: The two lists differ in which legions are named, not only in wording. The Latin is followed. On the word vexilla (detachments), see the entry at 2:18: Church and Brodribb's 'veteran troops' is a possible sense of the Latin.
